survey Q/A scaffolding for transforms answer

spans.assertion: the data were restructured so that a single match (one game for a given player-referee pair) was one observation, obtained by duplicating each original player-referee row by the number of games that pair had together
a binary variable 'red' was constructed: set to 1 for the number of rows equal to the sum of that pair's yellowRed and redCards counts, and 0 for the remaining rows
the 'red' variable was used as the dependent variable in all models
a variable for each player's average number of goals per game was computed
the average-goals-per-game variable was standardized
average goals was computed using all of a player's matches rather than only matches with the specific referee, to avoid a confound between red cards and goals
birthday was transformed into age in days
the age-in-days variable was standardized
six playing positions were recoded into three by dropping side-of-field information (e.g. left/right winger merged into 'winger'), since side was judged irrelevant to red cards
height, weight, meanIAT, and meanExp variables were standardized
standardization of meanIAT and meanExp used only countries retained in the subsequent analysis, i.e. those whose measure's standard error was below 1/5 of the SD of mean values
rater1 and rater2 were averaged to form the rating variable
the rater-average rating variable was standardized
the rating standardization was computed at the player level rather than the match level, to aid interpretation

spans.note: survey Q/A scaffolding for exclusions answer

spans.assertion: cases with missing values on any predictor used in a given model were excluded
for models using meanIAT and meanExp, observations for referees from countries whose measure's standard error exceeded 1/5 of the SD of mean values across countries were excluded
the 1/5-of-SD exclusion threshold was chosen arbitrarily
that threshold meant referees from countries where the attitude measure was computed from about 25 people or fewer were removed from the analysis
this exclusion was performed so results would not be influenced by unreliable attitude-measure values

spans.note: survey Q/A scaffolding for technique answer

spans.assertion: multilevel linear modelling was used as the statistical technique

spans.note: survey Q/A scaffolding for technique explanation
generic description of what multilevel modelling does (accounts for hierarchical data structure), not a dataset-specific action

spans.assertion: the multilevel model captures effects of individual players and referees in this dataset

spans.note: survey Q/A scaffolding for technique references
Baguley 2012; Bates, Maechler & Bolker 2012; Gelman & Hill 2007
survey Q/A scaffolding for software answer

spans.assertion: the analysis was run in R 3.0.2 using the lme4 package version 1.1.6

spans.note: survey Q/A scaffolding for outcome distribution answer

spans.assertion: the red-card outcome variable was binary
multilevel logistic regression would have been the more appropriate technique given the binary outcome, but was not the one used
multilevel linear regression was used as the modeling approach
multilevel logistic regression was not used because it was too computationally intensive to run

spans.note: survey Q/A scaffolding for RQ1 covariates answer

spans.assertion: the RQ1 model included position, height, and weight as predictors
the RQ1 model included player and referee as random effects
age and average number of goals were dropped from the RQ1 predictors because they increased AIC

spans.note: survey Q/A scaffolding for RQ2a covariates answer

spans.assertion: the RQ2a model included position, height, weight, and meanIAT as predictors
the RQ2a model included player and referee as random effects

spans.note: survey Q/A scaffolding for RQ2b covariates answer

spans.assertion: the RQ2b model included position, height, weight, and meanExp as predictors
the RQ2b model included player and referee as random effects

spans.note: survey Q/A scaffolding for covariate rationale answer

spans.assertion: a full model containing all covariates was initially specified
covariates that increased AIC were subsequently discarded from the model
the RQ2a and RQ2b models were built from the RQ1 final model by adding meanIAT or meanExp and its interaction with average skin-color rating

spans.note: survey Q/A scaffolding for effect-size unit answer

spans.assertion: effect size was expressed as the percentage increase in probability of getting a red card per one-unit increase in the predictor
for RQ1, a one-unit increase corresponds to a one-standard-deviation increase in the predictor (skin-tone rating)
for RQ2a and RQ2b, the predictor is the interaction between standardized average skin-color rating and standardized meanIAT or meanExp of the referee's country of origin

spans.note: survey Q/A scaffolding for RQ1 effect size answer

spans.assertion: the effect size for RQ1 (player skin tone and red cards) was 0.0621, 95% CI [0.0187, 0.1055]

spans.note: survey Q/A scaffolding for RQ2a effect size answer

spans.assertion: the effect size for RQ2a (referee-country implicit prejudice and red cards) was 0.0091, 95% CI [-0.1090, 0.1271]

spans.note: survey Q/A scaffolding for RQ2b effect size answer

spans.assertion: the effect size for RQ2b (referee-country explicit prejudice and red cards) was 0.0466, 95% CI [-0.0592, 0.1523]

spans.note: survey Q/A scaffolding for alternative analyses answer

spans.assertion: an ordinary (non-hierarchical) linear regression was run for initial exploration of the data
multilevel logistic regression was attempted and found not possible to run in reasonable time
models with additional levels of random effects (e.g. player within club within league) were tried
the additional-random-effects-level models performed worse in terms of AIC than the model used
